prime.problem: Every card in this series says "you should see" and prints exact numbers. If your Python, torch version, device or random generator differs from the one those numbers came from, you can't tell a bug in your code from a difference in your setup.
prime.fits: This is the ground floor of the toolkit, next to the Python card. Every later lab assumes this environment, and the cpu-vs-mps choice made here comes back in the GPT and GPT-2 lectures.
expect: which lecture needs a rented GPU
prime.goal: Build the course environment, prove it works in one run, and pick the right device for any lecture with a reason.

attend: If the M3 has a GPU, why do the makemore lectures deliberately stay on the CPU?
What exactly does a seed pin down, and what can still change the numbers you see?
Which single run in the whole course is out of reach for a laptop, and what ratio makes it so?
Why pin torch==2.14.0 instead of installing whatever is newest?

must: A seed fixes the stream of one generator → the CPU and MPS generators are different streams → same seed on mps gives [0.9843, …] instead of the notebook's [0.7081, …] → stay on cpu when you want to check against the notebooks

Seeded draws also depend on how each torch function consumes the stream → that can change between versions → pin torch 2.14.0 so your output matches the cards, and expect some video samples (mor. vs cexze.) to differ anyway

Makemore nets are small and every lab finishes in minutes on the CPU → nothing to gain by giving up notebook-matching draws; GPTs spend their time in big matmuls, where mps ran a 2048×2048 matmul 1.7–2.5× faster → cpu for L1–L6, mps for L7 and GPT-2
The GPT-2 run is 10B tokens → about 1,300 tok/s on the M3 vs about 1.5M tok/s on 8×A100 → about 89 days vs about 1.9 h → rent a GPU for that one run only
elevated: An isolated venv owns its own Python and packages → nothing from other projects leaks in → when a lab prints a different version, you know the environment, not your code, is the difference
reference: the exact uv venv / uv pip install commands and the repo list
extra packages for later lectures: graphviz (+ brew install graphviz), transformers, datasets, tqdm, requests
the dataset sizes: names.txt 32,033 lines, input.txt 1,115,394 characters
the matmul timings (27.4 ms cpu, 10.9 ms mps under load; they vary run to run)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how you'd set up for the course and how you'd choose a device for a given lecture. Or draw the "which lecture?" decision with its three outcomes and one reason on each arrow.
checklist: one isolated Python 3.10 venv with torch 2.14.0, numpy, matplotlib, jupyter, tiktoken, plus Karpathy's repos and the two datasets
a single check script proves versions, MPS, data and a known seeded draw
cpu for the small makemore nets, because the CPU generator reproduces the notebooks
mps for GPT work, where the matmuls are big
a rented CUDA GPU only for GPT-2's 10B-token run

retrieve.q: Explain why the same seed can give different numbers on cpu and on mps, and why that matters for following the lectures.
answer: a seed initialises one specific generator; each device has its own generator with its own stream
the notebooks used the CPU generator, so only it reproduces their draws
different draws mean different initial weights and samples, so losses stop lining up

retrieve.q: Walk through what labs/setup-m3.py checks, in order, and what a wrong value at each step would tell you.
answer: Python version and arm64 (x86_64 would mean Rosetta)
torch 2.14.0 and numpy versions (a different torch can change seeded outputs)
mps built/available True, cuda False
both data files present with the expected sizes
a matmul on each device actually runs
the seeded draw equals [0.7081, 0.3542, 0.1054]

retrieve.q: A friend wants to do the whole GPT-2 lecture on their M3. What can they do locally, what can't they, and what would you tell them to rent?
answer: loading, sampling, overfitting a batch, the loss check and the HellaSwag eval all run on mps (the full eval took 1052 s)
the 10B-token pretraining run would take about 89 days at ~1,300 tok/s
rent 8×A100 for that run only: about 1.9 h at ~1.5M tok/s
memory caps batches too: B=4, T=1024 was the practical ceiling in 24 GB

compare.q: That card samples with a seeded torch.Generator and matches the notebook exactly. This card shows a seed that doesn't. What's the design difference between the two cases, and how would you tell which one you're in?
answer: both use seed 2147483647; the match needs the same generator type (CPU) and the same consumption pattern
that card stays on the CPU generator and torch 2.14 consumes it the same way for rand and multinomial
an mps generator is a different stream, so it fails
check by printing the first draw and comparing to a known value such as [0.7081, 0.3542, 0.1054]

compare.q: The bigram lecture's name samples differ from the video (cexze. vs mor.) even on the CPU generator. What changed if not the seed or the device, and how should that change what you trust on a card?
answer: the torch version: how a function turns the stream into samples can change between releases
so the seed and device match, and the output still differs
trust the numbers your lab printed on torch 2.14, and read the video's as "same idea, different draws"

predict.q: You draw torch.rand(3) with the CPU generator (seed 2147483647) and then move the result to the GPU with .to('mps'). Commit first: do the values match the notebook's [0.7081, 0.3542, 0.1054]? And what happens if you pass the CPU generator straight to torch.rand(3, generator=g, device='mps')?
predict.answer: The moved tensor matches exactly: [0.7081, 0.3542, 0.1054], because the numbers were drawn on the CPU and only copied. Passing the CPU generator with device='mps' raises RuntimeError: Expected a 'mps' device type for generator but found 'cpu' (both measured on your M3, torch 2.14). So one way to get notebook-identical random init for a model on mps is to draw on the CPU and then move it.

apply.task: Design question: estimate the GPT-2 (124M) pretraining run on two setups. It is 19,073 steps of 2<sup>19</sup> tokens. Compute the total tokens, then the time at about 1,300 tok/s (your M3, measured) and at about 1.5M tok/s (8×A100, from the video). Then write one sentence on which parts of the lecture you'd run locally and which you'd rent for.
apply.done: You get 19,073 × 524,288 = 10.00B tokens, about 2,137 h ≈ 89 days on the M3, and about 1.9 h on 8×A100, matching the GPT-2 course's labs/results.py output.
apply.hint: 10.00e9 / 1,300 s, then divide by 3,600 and by 24. Do the same with 1.5e6.
